strengths: Addresses important practical problem of anytime NAS for tabular data with clear cloud-resource-budget motivation
NAS-Bench-Tabular benchmark with 160K architectures is a valuable contribution for future research
Comprehensive empirical evaluation of 9 existing zero-cost proxies on tabular data, demonstrating ExpressFlow superiority
Two-phase system design is well-motivated and clearly formulated with explicit time allocation constraints
Strong experimental results showing significant speedups (up to 82.75x) and consistent anytime capability
Excellent reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, extensive ablations (Appendices D-F), promised code release
Thorough theoretical analysis of ExpressFlow combining trainability and expressivity considerations
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: filtering phase uses standard Regularized Evolution, refinement uses standard Successive Halving, ExpressFlow combines existing concepts; primary contribution is engineering combination
Narrow evaluation scope: only 3 binary classification datasets, no regression/multi-class tasks, limited to simple fully-connected architectures (L=4 fixed), search space of 160K is modest

Insufficient theoretical justification for key design choices: K_l/ℓ(z_l) weighting appears ad-hoc, neuron saliency vs parameter saliency justification weak, data-agnostic property requiring artificial all-one vectors is questionable
Limited transferability evidence: ExpressFlow only evaluated on 3 similar tabular datasets; image data results (Table 15) show it ranks 2nd not 1st, raising generalization concerns
Weak baseline comparisons: one-shot NAS uses only basic weight-sharing (SRCC 0.12), TabNAS comparison in Table 11 shows small gaps, missing recent NAS method comparisons
Coordinator design lacks theoretical grounding: M/K≈30 and U=2 determined empirically, no explanation for why these values work; objective function is constraint-based not optimization-based
Statistical rigor issues: results report medians without confidence intervals; no discussion of variance across seeds; batch size stability (Appendix D) unexplained
Missing critical ablations: no clear isolation of filtering phase, refinement phase, and coordinator contributions; Table 11 compares only filtering+refinement combination

strengths: Comprehensive experimental study with extensive ablations and multiple baselines
Well-organized paper with detailed appendices addressing methodological details
Useful benchmark contribution (NAS-Bench-Tabular) for tabular data research
Solid engineering of two-phase optimization scheme with clear empirical validation
Good reproducibility practices including best practices checklist and hyperparameter documentation
weaknesses: Limited novelty: ExpressFlow combines existing concepts (neuron saliency, trajectory length) with ad-hoc recalibration weights; two-phase approach is not new (Abdelfattah et al. 2021 explored similar combinations)
Critical result in Figure 5 reveals filtering phase failure: higher ExpressFlow scores do not correlate with better AUC, fundamentally undermining the approach
Highly inconsistent and unreliable results: speedups vary from 1.75x to 82.75x across datasets, indicating poor generalizability and problem-dependence

Severely constrained search space: only 4 fixed-depth layers with 20 layer sizes, 160K total architectures—much smaller than modern tabular NAS which explores richer spaces (connections, feature interactions, heterogeneous layers)

Extremely limited evaluation scope: only 3 datasets all with binary classification and relatively small sizes; no regression, multiclass, or imbalanced problems; cannot support generalizability claims

ExpressFlow design appears ad-hoc: parameter positivity requirement (w=|w|) is a workaround; data-agnostic property using all-one vectors is suspicious and suggests proxy captures limited information; recalibration scheme K_l/ℓ(z^l) lacks principled justification
Modest technical improvements: SRCC gains over existing proxies are marginal (0.82 vs 0.77); coordinator constants (M/K≈30, U=2) determined empirically on three datasets with unclear generalization
Questionable 'anytime' claim: only tests discrete time budgets without demonstrating smooth improvement curves or adaptive behavior; coordinator uses fixed ratios rather than true adaptation
Search space design not justified: why 4 layers, why these specific sizes, why only binary classification; no sensitivity analysis

strengths: First anytime NAS approach for tabular data addressing a genuinely under-explored problem with practical applications in resource-constrained settings
Strong empirical results demonstrating 82.75× speedup over RE-NAS and consistent performance improvements across three diverse tabular datasets
Significant community contribution: NAS-Bench-Tabular benchmark with 160,000 pre-evaluated architectures enables future research without expensive re-evaluation
ExpressFlow zero-cost proxy is well-motivated, theoretically grounded in neuron saliency theory, and shows superior correlation (0.82-0.90 SRCC) compared to 9 existing proxies across tabular datasets
Elegant two-phase optimization scheme combining training-free and training-based evaluation with principled budget-aware coordinator for time allocation

Comprehensive experimental evaluation with extensive ablation studies validating design choices (batch size, initialization, recalibration weights), sensitivity analysis on M/K and U, and data-agnostic property verification
Rigorous methodology following NAS best practices: clear mathematical formulation (Eq. 2), detailed hyperparameter specifications, reproducible setup with code/data release promised
Honest treatment of limitations: Figure 5 clearly demonstrates why filtering-only fails, motivating the two-phase design; Appendix E analyzes necessity of coordinator
weaknesses: Limited dataset diversity: only 3 tabular datasets tested; generalization to diverse tabular domains unclear, and no comprehensive UCI benchmark suite evaluation
Restricted search space: only optimizes layer sizes with fixed 4-layer architecture topology, limiting applicability to genuine architecture design; doesn't explore operations or hyperparameters

Unfair baseline comparisons: RE-NAS and TabNAS not designed for anytime scenarios; claims of 82.75× speedup conflate combining paradigms with anytime capability; missing comparisons to cost-aware methods (e.g., ASHA-based approaches) or equivalent time-budget versions

Incremental novelty: filtering uses standard Regularized Evolution + existing zero-cost proxies; refinement uses standard Successive Halving; main contribution is the combination and coordinator, which is a solid but somewhat limited algorithmic innovation

No theoretical analysis or guarantees: lack of bounds on solution quality within time budget; M/K ≈ 30 empirically fixed without principled justification or derivation; linear time model assumptions not validated

Insufficient investigation of systematic bias: ExpressFlow-AUC correlation gaps (Figure 5) demonstrated but not deeply analyzed; parameter positivity constraint (w = |w|) appears ad-hoc; limited to ReLU activations

Missing practical guidance: no discussion of when anytime NAS is preferred over simpler alternatives (e.g., gradient boosting); limited deployment considerations; no framework for practitioners to choose M/K/U parameters
Unfair one-shot NAS comparison: weight-sharing shows low SRCC (0.12) but this deserves more discussion; relegated to appendix despite being relevant baseline for tabular data
